steps: Unpack & inspect

Check the stove and parts for transit damage and report damaged or missing parts to the dealer. Remove the packaging in the flue collar; the box under the stove holds internal parts and their instruction sheet.

Pack list: the stove and the owner's manual. The safety label hangs from a cable under the stove. Don't damage the label or cable when lifting; after final positioning the label can be stored in the holding clip on the bottom shield.
Site the stove

Freestanding room heater only, never in a factory-built fireplace. Prefer a main living area over a basement or confined space, and check clearances to walls, floor, ceiling and chimney chase before connecting.
Floor protection
Continuous noncombustible protector under and beyond the stove: 41 1/2" x 40" min. (US), 45" x 50" min. (Canada). No insulated pad or R-value needed; check LVP/LVT flooring limits.
Clearances

Take wall and corner clearances from the lettered Figure 4 table (p. 10) for the connector and shield used; alcoves need 54.5" min. width and 61.5" min. ceiling. Trim and mantel per Figure 6 (p. 13); reduce only with an NFPA 211 system and AHJ approval.
Outside air (if used)

Kit 96-53400 to a 3" min. duct (4" adaptor 90-53308), terminated no higher than the stove's intake, screened and hooded. Mandatory in mobile homes; in Canada fasten the stove down and fit a damper allowing 100% closure.
Chimney connector

8" 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel, or listed double wall; no aluminum or galvanized. Crimped ends toward the stove, three #10 x 1/2" screws per joint including the flue collar, horizontal runs rising at least 1/4" per foot.

Keep it as short and straight as possible; long runs and extra elbows add draft resistance and creosote. It may not pass through a floor, ceiling, attic, roof space, closet or similar concealed space. A cleanout tee is recommended.

Through a combustible wall, use a thimble or pass-through per NFPA 211 or CAN/CSA-B365. P. 12 lists four approved methods, for example 3.5in brick with 12in of brick from the clay liner to combustibles, or a 24 gauge ventilated thimble separated from combustibles by 6in of glass fiber insulation.

Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct.
Chimney

Listed Type HT (2100° F) per UL 103 or ULC S629, or a code-approved lined masonry chimney (max. 8" round or 8" x 8" tile), not smaller than the flue collar. Top it 3 feet above the roof opening and 2 feet above any part of the roof within 10 feet.

Prefabricated: follow the chimney maker's instructions precisely, and buy the pass-through or ceiling support, tee, fire-stops, insulation shield, flashing and cap from the same maker. Interior chimneys draw better and collect less creosote than exterior ones.

Masonry

  • Have it inspected first and repair cracks, loose mortar or blockage. The cleanout door must seal tight.
  • Walls: mortared brick or block at least 4" thick, or mortared rubble or stone; a liner is required either way.
  • Liner: tile with a 5/8" min. wall, refractory mortar and 1" of air space, or a UL listed 8" stainless liner, insulated or wrapped (or the space filled with vermiculite).
  • Clearance to combustibles: 2" for an interior chimney (fire stops at floors and ceilings, insulation kept 2" away), 1" for an exterior one.
Check the draft
Measure at installation: the stove requires 0.06" to 0.1" WC. Above 0.1" WC, install a stovepipe damper; some installations need more than one.
Mobile home (if applicable)

Install per 24 CFR Part 3280 (HUD) with the outside air kit, the stove fastened to the floor with the shipping clips, and a listed mobile home chimney and connector kit with spark arrester. Never in a sleeping room.

• Kit (UL103 or ULC-S629): stainless spark arrester cap, storm collar, adjustable vented flashing 0/12 – 6/12, two 24" chimney pipes, 24" support box with built-in starter section and trim.
  • Chimney attached directly to the stove, at least 3 feet above the roof where it passes and 2 feet above any part of the home within 10 feet, mechanically secured to the ceiling support box.
  • Roof terminations removable at or below 13-1/2 feet above ground without special tools. A chimney exiting other than through the roof, 7 feet or less above ground, needs a guard up to 7 feet.
  • Maintain the structural integrity of walls, floor, ceiling and roof, and the vapor barrier. Remove the chimney when transporting the home.
Break-in & final check
First fires follow the break-in procedure: low and steady, warm not hot. Afterwards inspect, and clean if needed, the stovepipe and chimney; cool break-in flue gas can build creosote fast.

panels.title: Stove smokes
items: Operating technique → open the air fully a minute before opening the door, bypass open first
Cold chimney or reverse draft → preheat the chimney; briefly open a window in the room
Blocked chimney → check chimney and stovepipe for blockage or creosote
Oversized chimney → reline; undersized → draft inducer or new chimney; too short → lengthen
Air leaking into the chimney → seal connections and openings, check clean-out doors
Bypass not closed, or catalysts not working → close it in the active range; inspect and brush the catalysts
Another appliance on the flue → disconnect it and seal the openings

panels.title: Back-puffing or gas explosions
items: Operating technique → air fully open a minute before opening, and a few minutes after reloading; bypass open first
Extra low burn rate → burn the stove at a higher rate
Chimney down-draft → install a chimney cap
Excessive ash build-up → empty ash more often; avoid poor-quality or green wood

panels.title: Uncontrolled or short burn
items: Unsealed or open door → close it tightly or replace the gaskets
Air leaking around the glass gasket → replace the gasket
Excessive draft (over 0.1 WC) → check the installation, low burn, stovepipe damper(s)
Extra long chimney → shorten it or install damper(s)
Oversized chimney → reline to the proper diameter
High winds or hilltop location → install a chimney cap

panels.title: Catalyst problems
items: Fly ash on the catalysts (light-off not held, bypass closed too soon, cardboard or garbage burned) → brush cold, follow light-off steps
Plugging or masking from wet, pitchy or small wood without light-off → dry wood; hot fire, then one hour high in the upper range
Warping or bowing from long periods too hot → lower air setting, keep in the operating zone

light.title: Lighting an everyday fire
light.html:
New stove? Do the break-in fire first. For every fire after that:

  1. Open the bypass handle (point it to the front). Open the door and put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox.
  2. Arrange about 10 pieces of kindling in a tee-pee over the paper. Each should be about 1/2" thick and 10" to 16" long.
  3. Pull the primary air lever all the way out.
  4. Light the paper under the kindling. Leave the door slightly open until the kindling catches and the draft starts to pull, then close it.
  5. Once the kindling is burning, add logs, small ones first. Keep them toward the center, away from the glass.
  6. When the fire is burning well and the catalyst thermometer reads Active, close the bypass (point it to the rear).
  7. Let it run on high for around 20 minutes, then set the air lever for the heat you want.
Slow to draw? In early fall, late spring or on muggy days, use small kindling for a quick, hot fire and briefly open a window in the room.
Burn the fire right on the firebox floor, with no grate. Never use gasoline, lantern fuel, kerosene, charcoal lighter fluid or similar liquids to start or freshen up a fire.

controls.title: Air control, bypass & thermometer
controls.html:
This is a catalytic stove: the catalysts burn up smoke the fire leaves behind. The bypass sends smoke around them or through them, and the thermometer tells you which to use.

Primary air lever

It's under the ash lip. Pull it out for more air, a faster burn and more heat. Push it in for a slower burn and less heat. It never closes completely.

Bypass handle

  • Pointing to the front: open. Smoke goes around the catalysts. Use this when you start a fire, and always before you open the door.
  • Pointing to the rear: closed. Smoke goes through the catalysts. Close it once they're up to temperature, and keep it closed while the stove burns in that range.

Catalyst thermometer

Inactivekeep the bypass open until the stove heats up
Activeclose the bypass
Too Hotkeep the door closed, push the air lever all the way in, let it cool to Active

The stove typically runs between 800 °F and 1300 °F.

Door

Pull the wood handle up and swing the door open. To latch it, push the door tight to the firebox, then push the handle in and down until it latches. Pull gently to check. Wear fireplace gloves when the stove is hot.

breakin.title: Break-in fires & first smells
breakin.html:
Soapstone has to be seasoned slowly. Over-firing a new stove can crack the stone or damage other parts. Build your first fire, and the first fire of every season, like this:

  1. Open the bypass. Put five or six double sheets of tightly twisted newspaper in the center of the firebox, with about ten pieces of kindling (1/2" thick, 10" to 16" long) crisscrossed on top.
  2. Pull the air lever all the way out and light the paper. Leave the door slightly open for a moment until the kindling catches, then close it.
  3. Keep a steady, low fire. The stove should feel warm, not hot. Add a few small chunks of wood at most.
  4. Once it's warm but not hot to the touch, push the air lever all the way in and let the fire die out.
  5. Let the stove return to room temperature.
Too hot: visible steam, boiling moisture or hissing means the soapstone is too hot.

Smoke and smells at first

The first fires give off some smoke and fumes as the paint and oils cure. Open a few windows; it usually fades after 10 to 20 minutes. The first fires each season can also smell of dust, pet hair or cleaners near the stove. If an odor persists, call your dealer.

Afterward, check the stovepipe and chimney and clean them if needed. Cool break-in fires can build creosote fast.

reload.title: Reloading & burn rates
reload.html:
Reloading

  1. Open the bypass, and pull the air lever fully out about a minute before you open the door.
  2. Open the door just a crack, pause so the smoke clears, then open it fully.
  3. Load onto a bed of hot, red coals. Logs can be up to 23" long. Leave a small valley in the coals behind the lower primary air opening so the new wood catches faster.
  4. Close the door and run it at a medium to high rate until the catalysts are back up to about 600 °F, then close the bypass.
Note: p. 24 says to run it at a medium to high rate for about 10 minutes after reloading a cool fire or one burned down to the charcoal stage; p. 30 says to run it with the air fully open for 15 to 20 minutes after reloading; p. 32 says to keep the air fully open for a few minutes after reloading.

Burn rates

Lowair lever all the way in
Medium-lowpulled out a little less than 1/4"
Medium-highpulled out a little less than 1/2"
Highall the way out

Medium-low is the typical setting and the best one when the stove is unattended. Long stretches on low build creosote. Never throw wood in or use the door to force it in.

wood.title: Choosing firewood
wood.html:
Burn only natural, untreated firewood (cordwood). Air-dried, seasoned hardwood gives higher efficiency and lower emissions than softwood or green wood.

  • Season it. Split, stack and air-dry green wood for a year. Seasoned wood is usually at or near 20% moisture; a hand-held moisture meter will tell you.
  • Stack it right. Keep the pile off the ground on skids or blocks and cover only the top. Tarps over the sides trap moisture.
  • Hard or soft? Softwoods burn hotter and faster. Hardwoods burn longer and leave better coals.

The manual ranks species by heat content: shagbark hickory, black locust and white oak are high; sugar maple, red oak and white ash medium high; paper birch and red maple medium; aspen, basswood and white cedar low.

Never burn

Garbage or trash, cardboard, paper products (including colored or glossy paper), plywood or particleboard, painted, treated (including pressure treated) or kiln-dried wood, unseasoned (green) wood, artificial or wax logs, compressed wood, coal, pellets, charcoal, lawn clippings, materials containing rubber (including tires), materials containing plastic, waste petroleum products, paints or paint thinners, solvents, asphalt products, materials containing asbestos, construction or demolition debris, railroad ties, manure or animal remains, driftwood (including salt water driftwood) or other previously salt water saturated materials, flammable fluids, highly volatile fuels or combustibles, or anything other than natural cordwood. Burning these materials may release toxic fumes, make the stove ineffective and cause smoke, or damage the catalysts. Fire starters made of paper, cardboard, sawdust or wax are fine for lighting.

Don't store firewood inside the stove's required clearances.

ash.title: Removing & disposing of ashes
ash.html:
Empty the ashes at the end of every week, sooner if the firebox is full. You can leave a thin layer in the firebox.

  1. Let the fire die down or go out completely.
  2. Push large live coals to the side and scoop out only the finer ash with a fireplace shovel.
  3. Don't let ash build up around the door opening. It can spill out, or pack into the gasket channel so the door won't seal.

Disposal

  • Put the ashes straight into a metal container with a tight-fitting lid. Put nothing else in it, and don't pour water in.
  • Set the closed container on a noncombustible floor or on the ground outside, well away from anything that burns, liquid fuels and vehicles. Never set it on a combustible surface or vinyl flooring.
  • Keep the ashes in the closed container until every coal is thoroughly cool, including before you bury or scatter them.
Never put ashes in wooden or plastic containers, in a trash can with other trash, or in paper or plastic bags. Coals in a bed of ashes can stay hot for several days.

glass.title: Cleaning the glass
glass.html:
The door glass is a tough ceramic made for wood stoves. Clean it only when the fire is out and the glass is cool.

  1. Dip a damp paper towel in gray ash and rub the inside of the glass in circles.
  2. When the deposits are gone, clean up with window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner, inside and out.
  3. Follow the cleaner's directions and wipe it off with a soft cloth or black-and-white newsprint.
Note: p. 30 suggests window cleaner or a commercial stove-glass cleaner, then says to use only a cleaner made specifically for woodstoves.
  • Never use a razor blade, steel wool or anything abrasive. Scratches weaken the glass.
  • Glass that's always dirty means the fire runs too cool or the wood is wet.
  • Never run the stove with cracked or broken glass, and don't slam the door. Your dealer has the replacement glass kit (96-58805).
Note: p. 29 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; p. 30 says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace the glass yourself.

care.title: Maintenance schedule
care.html:
Every day

Run the stove with the air lever fully out for 35 to 45 minutes to burn off creosote, the tar that builds up in the chimney and can catch fire. While the stove is new, check for creosote daily until you learn how fast it builds up.

Every other month

  • Look over the stovepipe and chimney. If more than 1/8" of creosote builds up, have it removed.
  • Do the dollar-bill test: with the stove cool, close the door on a dollar bill. If it pulls out with no resistance, the door isn't sealing. Adjust the latch or replace the gasket.
  • Brush fly ash and soot off the face of the catalysts with a soft-bristled brush. Check them at least three times a heating season.

End of every season

  • Take the stovepipe apart, clean it and replace rusted pieces. Inspect and clean the chimney.
  • Clean out the stove, and the catalysts if needed.
  • Replace door gaskets that are worn, frayed, cracked or very hard. Plan on new ones every two to three seasons.
Before each heating season, have the whole system professionally inspected, cleaned and repaired if needed. A certified chimney sweep is recommended.

safety.title: Safety & chimney fires
safety.html:
If you have a chimney fire

  1. If the fire is too threatening, leave and call the fire department right away.
  2. Otherwise, close the primary air control, the stovepipe damper (if you have one) and the bypass.
  3. Keep the front door closed.
Never throw water on the stove, stovepipe or chimney. The instant steam can cause serious harm.

Once the chimney fire is out, leave the air control and bypass closed and let the fire in the stove die out. Inspect the stove, stovepipe and chimney, and fix any damage before you use it again.

Signs of over-firing

Never over-fire your stove. It damages the stove. Watch for warped parts, short burn times, a roaring sound in the stove or stovepipe, or a discolored stovepipe. If you suspect it, stop using the stove and call your dealer immediately. Over-firing damage isn't covered by the warranty.

Every day

  • Keep furniture, drapes, clothing and other combustibles at least 36" away.
  • Keep children and pets away while it burns.
  • Keep the front door closed except to light and load.
  • Install smoke and CO detectors, and keep an "A B C" fire extinguisher handy.

warranty.title: Warranty at a glance
warranty.html:
Hearthstone covers the original retail purchaser only, when an authorized Hearthstone dealer (or their representative) installed the stove. Coverage starts on the original invoice date and can't be transferred. "Limited Lifetime" means 10 years.

Stone; cast iron not listed elsewhereLimited Lifetime
Door handles and latches; steel components and firebox5 years
Electrical and gas components2 years
Enamel finish, accessories, glass, all components not listed elsewhere1 year

Rows checked for only some fuel types are on the grid on p. 37.

Note: the warranty grid on p. 37 covers glass for 1 year, but exclusion 3 on p. 38 lists glass among the wear parts the warranty doesn't cover.

Catalysts

Their maker, Applied Ceramics, replaces them free if they stop working within two years, then at a prorated price ($130.00 in year 3 up to $160.00 in year 6). Keep your bill of sale.

Note: p. 36 gives the catalysts' free-replacement period as two (2) years, then mentions replacement catalysts "during the three year period."

Not covered

Over-firing, wrong fuels, not following the manual, wear parts such as gaskets and paint, and work by anyone but an authorized dealer. To claim, contact your Hearthstone dealer.

specOutput.title: Output, efficiency & emissions
specOutput.html:
Max heat output80,000 BTU/hr (cordwood, independent lab)
EPA test output range15,069 – 33,396 Btu
Weighted efficiency81% (HHV)
Particulate0.7 g/hr (EPA 2020 standard, crib wood)
CO, Cat 1 / 2 / 3 / 412.6 / 13.8 / 9.6 / 18.0 g/hr
Heated areaup to 2,500 sq ft

Tested to EPA Method 28R (40 CFR Part 60); efficiency is the weighted average of the 4 burn rate categories (EPA Method 28R and CSA B415-10). The minimum low burn rate is set at the factory and must not be altered (federal regulation).

The manual's rating notes print the emission rate as "0.7 gr/hr." (p. 2); its spec page (p. 7) gives 0.7 g/hr.

specFirebox.title: Firebox & fuel
specFirebox.html:
Firebox capacity3.1 cu ft
Max log length23" (58.4cm)
Burn timeup to 24+ hrs (Heat Life up to 30 hours)
Wood per cu ft of firebox10 to 25 lbs, by species, moisture and packing
CatalystApplied Ceramics ACI-6M2, three cartridges

Natural cordwood only, burned directly on the firebox floor (no grate). The catalysts sit behind the cast iron catalyst access cover at the back of the stove; replacement kit 96-75800. Never operate the stove without the catalysts.

specFlue.title: Connector & chimney
specFlue.html:
Connector8" (203 mm) dia., 24 MSG or 25 MSG blued steel, or listed double wall
Metal chimney8" (203 mm) ID, Type HT (2100° F), UL 103 or ULC S629
Masonry chimney8" round or 8" x 8" square flue, lined
Chimney linerUL 1777 or ULC S635
Flue sizingnot less than the flue collar, not more than three times its area

No aluminum or galvanized pipe. Double-wall connectors named: Simpson DuraVent DVL and Metalbestos DS (Security, GSW and Ameritec also acceptable); the manual's double-wall clearances are specific to DuraVent DVL. Never connect to a flue serving another appliance or to any air distribution duct.

The manual also prints 8" as 152 mm for the connector stovepipe (p. 14) and the prefabricated chimney flue (p. 15); its spec page (p. 7) gives 8" (203 mm).

specDraft.title: Draft & chimney height
specDraft.html:
Required draft0.06" – 0.1" WC
Above 0.1" WCinstall a stovepipe damper
Rec. min. height, top exit16 feet off the floor (13 feet 5 inches from stove top)
Rec. min. height, rear exit19 feet off the floor (16 feet 5 inches from stove top)
Rec. max. height30 feet
Above the roof3 feet above the roof opening; 2 feet above any roof within 10 feet
Maker's website: Flue Exit Location Top. Install to the manual.

Check the draft at installation; a tall chimney can over-draft, and some installations need more than one damper. To confirm heat output, a 400° F stovepipe reading no more than 12 inches above the flue collar shows the stove is supplying sufficient heat. For low heat the chart on p. 32 lists low-Btu or green wood, a low burn rate, a cold exterior chimney, leaky stovepipe or chimney, and house heat loss.

specClear.title: Clearances to combustibles
specClear.html:
Furniture, drapes, wood, paper36" (92 cm) min.
Min. alcove width54.5" (138.4cm)
Min. alcove ceiling from floor61.5" (156.2cm), single or double wall connector
Protected surfacessee NFPA 211

Wall and corner clearances are lettered dimensions (A–F) defined on the Figure 4 drawing (p. 10), one row per connector (single or double wall) and shield (included rear heat shield, or blower kit shield from kit #96-57800), for parallel, corner and alcove installs. Through-the-wall connector clearances are lettered on Figure 5 (p. 11), and trim and mantel clearances are a drawing only (Figure 6, p. 13). Read the values off those drawings.

Maker's website: Clearances Side 13"; Rear 8" (single-wall connector) / 5" (double-wall with blower); Corner 7". Install to the clearance diagrams in the manual.

Dimensions are from the stove body. Double-wall pipe clearance to the ceiling follows the pipe maker's specifications. Reduce clearances only with an NFPA-approved wall protection system and approval of the authority having jurisdiction.

specFloor.title: Floor protection
specFloor.html:
US minimum41 1/2" x 40"
Canada minimum45" x 50"
Insulated hearth padnot required (no R-value requirement)

On a combustible floor, use a continuous noncombustible protector (tile, brick, slate, glass or similar facing) under the stove and extending beyond it. The extension on each side is shown only on the Figure 3 drawing (p. 9).

Some LVP and LVT flooring begins to warp at 110° Fahrenheit. Check the flooring maker's limits; extra shielding may be needed.

specSize.html:

specAir.title: Outside air supply
specAir.html:
Outside air kit96-53400, attaches under the stove
Duct3" (76 mm) min. diameter, supplied by others
4" duct adaptorkit #90-53308
Terminationno higher than the stove's air intake

The IRC doesn't allow the duct to terminate higher than the appliance; Hearthstone recommends the same level or lower. Place it where snow or leaves can't block it, with ¼" x ¼" mesh rodent screen and a rain/wind proof hood. Required in all mobile homes. In Canada, fasten the stove to the floor with the shipping clips and fit a damper allowing 100% closure.

Consider it when the stove doesn't draw steadily, smoke rolls out, other fuel-fired equipment back-drafts, or the house is tightly sealed or has devices that exhaust house air.

conflicts.issue: Metric size of the 8" connector/flue: 8" (203 mm) on p. 7 (connector, metal chimney, masonry chimney) but 8" (152 mm) on p. 14 (connector stovepipe) and p. 15 (prefabricated chimney flue). The inch value agrees.
Particulate emission rate unit: 0.7 g/hr in the specifications (p. 7) vs "0.7 gr/hr." in the rating notes (p. 2).

How long to run hot after reloading: about 10 minutes at a medium to high rate for a cool fire or one burned to the charcoal phase (p. 24); 15 to 20 minutes with the primary air fully open (p. 30); a few minutes with the air fully open (p. 32, back-puffing).
Glass cleaner: p. 30 says to clean up with window cleaner or commercial stove glass cleaners, then says to use a cleaner specifically manufactured for woodstoves only.
Who replaces broken glass: p. 29 says only a qualified service person should replace the glass panel; p. 30 says to wear work gloves and safety glasses if you replace the glass yourself.
Glass coverage: the components grid lists glass under 1 Year for all fuels (p. 37), but exclusion 3 lists glass among wear parts not covered (p. 38).

Catalyst warranty: no-charge replacement within two (2) years of purchase, prorated from Year 3, but the same page refers to one replacement per defective catalyst returned "during the three year period" (p. 36).

catalog_mismatches.catalog: Side 13"; Rear 8" (single-wall connector) / 5" (double-wall with blower); Corner 7"
catalog_mismatches.manual: Figure 4 table, lettered A-F (letters defined only on the drawing): A 13", B 8", C 13", D 28", E 7", F 20.5"; double wall connector with blower kit shield (not alcove): B 5", C 10"
Recommended chimney heights given for a top of stove installation and for a rear exit connection (p. 16); Figure 5 shows a through the wall top flue exit (p. 11)

review.notes: Catalog specs all match the manual (80,000 BTU/hr, 2,500 sq ft, 81% HHV, 0.7 g/hr, 3.1 cu ft, 23" logs, 8" flue, 33" x 29-1/2" x 24-1/8", 550 lbs., burn time up to 24+ hrs, blower and outside air optional, mobile home section present). Wall/corner/alcove clearances (A-F, p. 10) and through-the-wall connector clearances (A-B, Figure 5, p. 11) are lettered dimensions defined only in the drawings, so their values were not transcribed; the catalog's side/rear/corner reading (13", 8"/5", 7") matches numbers in that table but the letter mapping can't be verified from the text. Diagram-only content not transcribed: dimension drawing (Fig. 1, p. 7), floor protector extensions (Fig. 3, p. 9), trim and mantel clearances (Fig. 6, p. 13), chimney configurations (Fig. 9, p. 17), acceptable catalyst distortion (Fig. 20, p. 28). The safety label page (p. 35) has no extractable text. Warranty grid (p. 37): only rows checked in all three fuel columns were summarized; rows with one or two checks (clean burning air supply system, burner and logs, burn pot and baffles, refractory/vermiculite panels/baffles, ash grate) can't be assigned to a fuel column from the text. Not flagged (inch values used, metric omitted): 16" kindling given as 457 mm for the break-in fire and 406 mm for everyday fires (p. 23); 10" given as 26cm (p. 10) and 25 cm (p. 11). p. 18 warns other fuels could generate dangerous levels of carbon monoxide, p. 21 says unauthorized fuel such as coal could produce high levels of carbon dioxide; owner text doesn't name the gas. The troubleshooting chart (p. 32) says to empty the ash pan and p. 25 mentions ash doors, but the ash section (p. 25) describes shoveling ash out of the firebox; no ash pan is described, so the guide says 'empty ash'. The Too Hot instruction (p. 21) says fully close the air control while p. 20 says the control doesn't close completely; written as pushing the lever all the way in.
